title: Framber Valdez, A.J. Hinch suspended in fallout from benches-clearing incident
content:
DETROIT — The past 24 hours in Detroit have been chaotic. There was Framber Valdez’s 94-mph fastball — his lone four-seam fastball of the 2026 season — that hit Trevor Story square in the back and spurred the benches to clear. There was the news Valdez received a six-game suspension, which was later reduced to five.

Tigers manager A.J. Hinch was also fined and suspended one game as a result of what Major League Baseball deemed “Valdez’s intentional actions.”

And Tuesday night, a video from former MLB player Eric Hosmer prompted further speculation about what exactly was going on in that night’s game. Hosmer’s video showed evidence the Red Sox might have been identifying pitch grips from Valdez’s glove and relaying signs to hitters when a runner was on second base. Story, who stole second in Boston’s three-run first inning, was among the players who might have been relaying signs.

“This is why Story ended up getting drilled,” Hosmer said in the video.

Whether possible pitch-tipping was the actual reason for Valdez’s meltdown is, of course, highly unclear. He plunked Story shortly after giving up back-to-back solo home runs to Willson Contreras and Wilyer Abreu in the fourth inning on Tuesday. Both hitters, Contreras in particular, admired their shots before beginning their trots around the bases. And of course, there was no runner on base when Valdez threw those pitches. Valdez surrendered 10 runs, seven of them earned, before his ejection.

After the game, Valdez claimed the pitch that hit Story was not thrown with intent. He said he chose to throw his lone four-seamer of the year after dissatisfaction with the horizontal movement on his sinker. He also seemed uncertain whether the Red Sox might have been relaying signs, though he admitted the thought crossed his mind.

“If they got something on me that I was tipping my pitches, of course that would be good for them, because I wasn’t doing my job,” Valdez said through an interpreter. “Honestly, that’s stuff that happens in the game. I got to go back and watch video, watch my performance and how my body was moving (to see) if they had something on me.”

Wednesday afternoon, Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler was aware of the speculation but echoed a similar sentiment.

“I didn’t really notice anything crazy out of the ordinary,” Dingler said. “They did a great job hitting. Every pitch got hit. So it wouldn’t surprise me, but in real time, no.”

Dingler said he is only able to pay so much attention to whether his pitcher might be tipping. The Tigers have coaches and staff members who help monitor such issues. But Dingler also looks out at runners on second to see if they might be picking up pitches or locations from his own setup.

“I see if the guy is moving at second base, moving with my location or after I move, if I see him do something, that’s something I can fix,” Dingler said. “I can set up later or try to deke a little bit.”

Relaying signs is part of the cat-and-mouse game between teams. It is generally within the rules so long as technology is not being used to relay information to the field in real-time. The influx of camera systems like KinaTrax, however, has increased the paranoia with which pitchers operate. Teams can decode tiny movements from previous starts, go over such footage in pregame meetings and use that knowledge to generate tips in that night’s game. The Red Sox tend to be regarded as one of the league’s most savvy teams when it comes to picking up tips.

Such intrigue and espionage often becomes a conversation on broadcasts or online. But even if the Red Sox had something on Valdez, it’s unclear if he knew in the moment. And even if Valdez did, there was other frustration that could have  prompted the pitch that resulted in a five-game suspension and further hurt a Tigers team that can hardly afford it.

“I assume always that everybody in the league works toward finding the glove tips and things like that,” Hinch said. “I don’t have any idea whether they were. It’s all fair. The best way to combat that is to clean up your own glove and your own pitches. But if they were, then that still falls on us.”
